title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows
authors: Tom Moussie, Pierric Joseph, Marcello Meldi
abstract: This work presents the development and assessment of a hybrid framework coupling numerical simulation, experimental samples, data assimilation (DA) and machine learning (ML) to investigate the flow within an axial compressor stage. The methodology first implements a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter (MFEnKF) which integrates experimental PIV data with a two-fidelity numerical simulation setup, combining steady-state RANS on a fixed grid with unsteady hybrid RANS/LES simulations on a moving grid. This data assimilation step successfully reduces discrepancies between experiments and CFD realizations. Besides, it provides additional high fidelity samples when compared with the available PIV data. This enriched database is used to train machine learning (ML) tools, with the objective to obtain black-box forcing terms to be included in the discretized form of the Navier-Stokes equations. These models are expected to preserve the accuracy of the DA results while not longer requiring the input of experimental data. The neural network architecture used here maps local physical features such as the velocity, the velocity gradients and the turbulent viscosity, to obtain the volume forcing terms. The analysis of the performance of such ML models shows that global accuracy is preserved but localized increased errors in specific regions of the compressor, such as close to the blade tips, can exceed those observed from the baseline RANS simulations. To resolve this issue, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) method is employed, which classifies and combines the trained ML tools for different flow regions. The discrepancy with experimental data of this method is systematically lower than the one observed for the baseline RANS solution and very similar to the one obtained with the MFEnKF.

infographic.key_insight: Region-aware Mixture of Experts models reproduce much of the accuracy gained through data assimilation in an axial compressor without requiring experimental inputs during deployment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learned forcing terms offer a route to improving turbomachinery CFD predictions beyond baseline RANS using experimentally informed corrections.
method: Fuse experimental PIV with steady fixed-grid RANS and unsteady moving-grid hybrid RANS/LES using a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter.
Train neural networks on the enriched database to map local velocity, velocity gradients and turbulent viscosity to discrete Navier–Stokes forcing terms.
Use a Mixture of Experts to combine learned corrections across different flow regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against experimental PIV, the Mixture of Experts yields systematically lower discrepancies than baseline RANS and results very similar to the assimilation solution.
infographic.watch_item: Individual neural models can exceed baseline RANS errors near blade tips; generalization beyond the studied compressor conditions is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows

title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
authors: Francesco Romor, Richard Schussnig, Charles A. Taylor, Gerhard A. Holzapfel, Alfonso Caiazzo
abstract: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.

infographic.key_insight: Shape-informed hemodynamic surrogates benefit most from active learning and physical consistency during fine-tuning, while generalization is limited primarily by geometric coverage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports scalable prediction of patient-specific aortic velocity and pressure fields toward real-time cardiovascular flow assessment.
method: Generate synthetic aortic CFD solutions with automatically adjusted, physiologically consistent boundary conditions.
Represent anatomies as displacement fields from a common reference and train Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogates.
Evaluate active learning and differentiable finite element residual constraints for data-efficient training and fine-tuning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Peak-systolic predictions and out-of-distribution studies show fine-tuning gains from gradient- and subspace-based acquisition and physical consistency, but the abstract reports no numerical accuracy metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Predictions for anatomies outside the geometric parametrization's support may remain unreliable regardless of network architecture.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics

title: Neural Operator Splitting for Fluid Dynamics in Complex Geometry
authors: Jianxiang Li, Xi Deng, Hong Chul Nam, Anima Anandkumar
abstract: Solving dynamical systems in complex and diverse geometries remains challenging for both numerical solvers and learning-based surrogate models. We propose Neural Operator Splitting, a framework for learning fluid dynamics while preserving the physical structure of fractional-step numerical schemes. Instead of learning the full-step evolution monolithically, we decompose each time step into physically interpretable steps, and learn each operator separately using intermediate states from the underlying numerical solver. Guided by the linearity properties of the fractional steps, we introduce a conditional-linear Fourier neural operator (CL-FNO) whose linear state mappings are modulated by nonlinear conditioning on inputs such as boundary geometry. We further introduce two complementary strategies, symmetry sampling and corrective cycling, to mitigate error accumulation during autoregressive rollout. Experiments on 2D and 3D fluid flows with varying geometries and initial conditions show that our full model reduces mean relative $L^2$ rollout error by 68\% in 2D and 40\% in 3D compared with a single full-step neural operator. At comparable error levels, neural-operator inference is approximately $10^3$ times faster per step than the Monte Carlo solver.

infographic.key_insight: Learning physically interpretable fractional-step operators separately improves fluid-flow predictions over a single full-step neural operator.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables fast CFD surrogate inference across varying geometries, with approximately 1,000× lower per-step inference time than the Monte Carlo solver at comparable error.
method: Split each time step into physical substeps and train separate operators using solver-generated intermediate states.
Use conditional-linear Fourier neural operators with linear state mappings conditioned nonlinearly on inputs such as boundary geometry.
Apply symmetry sampling and corrective cycling to mitigate autoregressive error accumulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on 2D and 3D flows with varying geometries and initial conditions report 68% and 40% reductions, respectively, in mean relative L2 rollout error versus a single full-step neural operator.
infographic.watch_item: Training requires access to solver-generated intermediate states, which may complicate integration with existing CFD pipelines.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Operator Splitting for Fluid Dynamics in Complex Geometry

title: DeHNSSo-v2: A compressible, curvilinear, and efficient extension of the Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver
authors: Pietro Carlo Boldini, Yifu Chen, Marios Kotsonis
abstract: We present DeHNSSo-v2, a major update of DeHNSSo-v1 (Westerbeek et al., Comput. Phys. Commun. 302, 2024), the open-source Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver for nonlinear stability analysis of shear flows. The new release adds a compressible formulation on general two-dimensional body-fitted geometries, automatic grid generation, linear-cost sparse assembly, reusable per-mode factorizations, and Newton pseudo-arclength continuation for high-amplitude nonlinear solutions. The curvilinear formulation preserves the fourth-order accuracy of the discretization on strongly distorted grids, and the compressible solver is confirmed to reproduce DeHNSSo-v1 in the incompressible limit. Validation spans published benchmarks for linear instability of compressible flat-plate boundary layers from $\mathrm{Ma}=0.5$ to $\mathrm{Ma}=4.5$, nonlinear oblique-mode breakdown at $\mathrm{Ma}=1.6$, nonlinear swept-wing crossflow compared with direct numerical simulations, and linear Tollmien-Schlichting wave interaction with a modeled surface-embedded Helmholtz resonator compared with experimentally validated linearized Navier-Stokes simulations. On the nonlinear test cases of DeHNSSo-v1, the computational developments result in a speed-up of approximately one order of magnitude. By broadening the scope and reducing the cost of DeHNSSo-v1, DeHNSSo-v2 provides the boundary-layer-transition and flow-control community with an accessible tool for studying receptivity, nonlinear disturbance evolution, and instability interactions with complex surface geometry and metamaterials across compressibility regimes.

infographic.key_insight: DeHNSSo-v2 extends nonlinear shear-flow stability analysis to compressible, body-fitted geometries while delivering approximately 10× speed-ups on DeHNSSo-v1 nonlinear test cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The open-source solver supports boundary-layer transition and flow-control studies involving complex surfaces, resonators, and compressibility effects.
method: Compressible formulation on general 2D curvilinear grids with automatic grid generation.
Linear-cost sparse assembly and reusable per-mode factorizations.
Newton pseudo-arclength continuation for high-amplitude nonlinear solutions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation covers linear boundary-layer instability at Mach 0.5–4.5, nonlinear breakdown at Mach 1.6, swept-wing crossflow against DNS, and modeled resonator interactions against experimentally validated simulations.
infographic.watch_item: The formulation uses two-dimensional body-fitted geometries; applicability to arbitrary fully three-dimensional geometries is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: DeHNSSo-v2: A compressible, curvilinear, and efficient extension of the Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver

title: Predicting trigger in streak breakdown via Picard-Chebyshev approach in plane-Poiseuille flow
authors: Nobutaka Taniguchi, Aiko Yakeno
abstract: The evolution of finite-amplitude disturbances is critical in the prediction of laminar-to-turbulent transition. To analyze the transient growth of disturbances, Pralits et al. (J. Fluid Mechanics, 2015) proposed a weakly nonlinear optimal perturbation (WNLOP) analysis that accounts for the effect of mean-flow distortion on the fundamental wave. The present study formulates a WNLOP analysis via Picard--Chebyshev iteration for compressible parallel flows to predict streak breakdown. The formulation incorporates the non-modal amplification of disturbances and their nonlinear interactions for polychromatic waves, considering all the possible nonlinear interactions starting from a finite set of initial wavenumber components. The nonlinear interaction is tracked as a monotonically increasing set of wavenumber components; specifically, the first-order approximation recovers the linear disturbance equation, the third-order approximation corresponds to the amplitude equation of weakly nonlinear theory, and further iterations systematically approach DNS results in the weakly nonlinear regime. By applying the proposed formulation to a subcritical plane Poiseuille flow at Mach number $\mathrm{M}=0.3$ and Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re}=3000$, the proposed formulation demonstrates high predictive accuracy in comparison with DNS calculations and succeeds in identifying the optimal perturbation restricted to a planar wave that causes streak breakdown in full nonlinear simulation. The proposed method predicts the nonlinear interaction between the streak and the planar wave, which generates an oblique wave and subsequent harmonic waves characterized by an alternating streamwise vortex structure, whose amplitude determines whether further nonlinear interactions are induced to trigger the turbulent transition.

infographic.key_insight: Picard–Chebyshev weakly nonlinear analysis predicts streak-breakdown triggers by tracking interactions that generate oblique and harmonic waves with alternating streamwise vortices.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support transition prediction by identifying finite-amplitude disturbances that destabilize otherwise laminar channel flow.
method: Formulate weakly nonlinear optimal perturbation analysis for compressible parallel flows using Picard–Chebyshev iteration.
Track non-modal amplification and nonlinear interactions across an expanding set of wavenumber components.
Progress from linear dynamics to weakly nonlinear amplitude equations and higher-order approximations.
infographic.evidence_signal: For subcritical plane Poiseuille flow at Mach 0.3 and Reynolds number 3000, the abstract reports high agreement with DNS and identifies a planar-wave perturbation that triggers streak breakdown in full nonlinear simulation.
infographic.watch_item: Demonstrated accuracy is limited to the reported flow conditions and weakly nonlinear regime; the expanding wavenumber set may increase computational cost.
infographic.paper_title: Predicting trigger in streak breakdown via Picard-Chebyshev approach in plane-Poiseuille flow

title: CuAD: Source-to-Source Automatic Differentiation of CUDA Kernels for Discrete Adjoints in Computational Fluid Dynamics
authors: Seunghyun Joo
abstract: Discrete adjoint methods give the sensitivities that aerodynamic design and data assimilation require, but they remain hard to obtain for flow solvers that run on graphics processors. This paper presents CuAD, a source-to-source automatic differentiation tool that reads CUDA kernels and writes their tangent and adjoint versions as ordinary CUDA source. Its reverse mode is organised around the GPU thread. It adopts the convention of CUDA kernels that inputs and outputs do not alias, recomputes intermediate values instead of storing them, differentiates pure accumulations without a tape and keeps any remaining tape in a fixed thread-local array. We evaluate CuAD on four kernels from simple flow models and on a two-dimensional Euler solver. All generated derivatives pass dot-product tests to round-off, and the adjoint kernels cost two to six times the primal kernels. On a Biot-Savart summation compiled by one compiler, the CuAD adjoint costs about four times the primal at every size, as does Enzyme when the source declares the absence of aliasing with __restrict__. On the unchanged source Enzyme caches the loop in the device heap and costs 9 to 240 times the primal, while the heap tape of Clad costs 60 to 4400 times the primal and fails beyond 8192 vortices. Exact Jacobians assembled from the generated tangents also matter for accuracy. In single precision, the adjoint gradient of a finite-difference Jacobian reaches errors of 45 to 75 per cent on a stiff Burgers problem and of $5\times10^{-4}$ to $4\times10^{-2}$ on a transonic airfoil, whereas the generated Jacobian keeps them below $5\times10^{-5}$ and $3\times10^{-6}$. The applications include the shape sensitivities of lift and drag of a transonic NACA 0012, for which the residual, the boundary conditions and the wall force are differentiated by CuAD and the adjoint agrees with the tangent to $10^{-13}$.

infographic.key_insight: CuAD transforms CUDA kernels into tangent and adjoint CUDA source, enabling accurate GPU-based sensitivities at an adjoint cost of two to six times the primal.
infographic.engineering_relevance: GPU-native discrete adjoints support aerodynamic shape optimization and data assimilation, including transonic airfoil lift and drag sensitivities.
method: Generate tangent and adjoint kernels through source-to-source automatic differentiation.
Organize reverse mode by GPU thread, assuming non-aliasing inputs and outputs.
Recompute intermediates, differentiate pure accumulations without a tape, and store remaining tape in fixed thread-local arrays.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four flow-model kernels and a 2D Euler solver, generated derivatives passed dot-product tests to round-off; transonic NACA 0012 adjoint and tangent sensitivities agreed to 10^-13.
infographic.watch_item: Applications must respect the non-aliasing convention and account for fixed thread-local tape requirements.
infographic.paper_title: CuAD: Source-to-Source Automatic Differentiation of CUDA Kernels for Discrete Adjoints in Computational Fluid Dynamics

title: Spatially developing drag reduction across a finite oscillating wall
authors: Marco Galli, Nicolò Scaiola, Ferdinand F. J. Schrijer, Fulvio Scarano
abstract: The spatial evolution of a turbulent boundary layer at $Re_τ= 652$ developing across a finite spanwise oscillating wall is investigated with normalised oscillation period of $T^+ \approx 101$ and amplitude $A^+ \approx 7$, yielding a drag reduction of 32\%. The spatial distribution of skin friction is estimated adopting a recently introduced near-wall data nonlinear regression method based on the arctangent function, which circumvents the requirement of high wall-normal resolution to capture the viscous sublayer. The method viability is assessed against reference DNS data, and the trends of measurement errors from experimental data are well reproduced. The local impact of the control action is examined by evaluating the spatial development of scalar fields of turbulence statistics as well as conditional quadrant analysis to link the onset and recovery transients to turbulence events. The boundary layer response is observed to follow an exponential decay law for the skin friction spatial evolution. The decay length-scale corresponds to $0.6$ boundary layer thicknesses $δ$ for the onset transient and $0.9δ$ for the recovery one. The same exponential fit applied to the Reynolds stresses yields a response within $0.5δ$, with the exception of the shear stress peak, that requires a significantly longer distance.

infographic.key_insight: A finite spanwise-oscillating wall achieves 32% drag reduction, with skin-friction onset and recovery following exponential responses over length scales of 0.6δ and 0.9δ, respectively.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These response lengths can inform the placement and sizing of finite wall-actuation patches for turbulent boundary-layer drag control.
method: Investigate a turbulent boundary layer at Reτ = 652 with oscillation period T+ ≈ 101 and amplitude A+ ≈ 7.
Estimate local skin friction using arctangent-based nonlinear regression of near-wall data.
Track turbulence statistics and conditional quadrant events across actuation onset and recovery.
infographic.evidence_signal: The skin-friction method was assessed against reference DNS data and reproduced experimental measurement-error trends; most Reynolds-stress responses had fitted length scales within 0.5δ, except the slower shear-stress peak.
infographic.watch_item: The reported performance is for one Reynolds number and actuation setting; net energy savings cannot be inferred without actuation-power data.
infographic.paper_title: Spatially developing drag reduction across a finite oscillating wall

title: Reynolds-number-dependent entrance bias in temperature polarization of lab-scale membrane distillation
authors: Soyoung Kim, Tiezheng Tong, Yinuo Noah Yao
abstract: Lab-scale membrane distillation (MD) modules are commonly used for membrane characterization and developing empirical heat-transfer correlations. Entrance-induced flow structures can introduce geometry-specific effects into measured temperature polarization (TP) and heat transfer. However, the dependence of these effects on module geometry and flow condition remains unclear. We performed three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of direct contact membrane distillation (DCMD) over inlet Reynolds numbers of $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}=10$-$1000$, focusing on side-chamber length and main-channel height. We discovered that counter-rotating streamwise vortices formed near the main-channel entrance across all geometries, but their downstream persistence increased with $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. At lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$, the vortices mostly decayed before mid-channel, while at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ they persisted farther downstream and produced pronounced spatial variations in TP. Increasing side-chamber length reduced the secondary-flow kinetic energy entering the main channel, and generally strengthened TP, whereas increasing main-channel height reduced the bulk velocity and streamwise kinetic energy, resulting in a thicker thermal boundary layer and stronger TP. For most geometries, the deviation from the straight-channel baseline changed from stronger TP at lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ to weaker TP at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. Entrance effects therefore vary in both magnitude and direction with operating condition and cannot be represented by a constant correction across the Reynolds-number range.

infographic.key_insight: Entrance-induced vortices create geometry-specific temperature-polarization bias whose magnitude and direction change with inlet Reynolds number.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lab-scale membrane characterization and heat-transfer correlations should account for inlet geometry and operating conditions rather than apply a constant entrance correction.
method: Three-dimensional CFD of direct contact membrane distillation.
Inlet Reynolds numbers from 10 to 1000.
Varied side-chamber length and main-channel height.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations found entrance vortices in all geometries, with greater downstream persistence at higher Reynolds numbers and, for most geometries, a shift from stronger to weaker temperature polarization relative to a straight-channel baseline.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports computational results without experimental validation; applicability beyond the simulated geometries and conditions requires testing.
infographic.paper_title: Reynolds-number-dependent entrance bias in temperature polarization of lab-scale membrane distillation

title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence
authors: B. Tripathi, A. E. Fraser, P. W. Terry, E. G. Zweibel, M. J. Pueschel, A. M. Beloborodov
abstract: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulent cross helicity can grow exponentially in sheared, inhomogeneous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence when shear-driven production exceeds effective losses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This instability may inform models of energy transfer and magnetic-field generation in conducting-fluid systems with strong shear.
method: Analytically derive the cross-helical shear instability.
Identify production by a nonzero Reynolds–Maxwell stress gradient.
Test the instability using three-dimensional numerical simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that three-dimensional simulations confirm the analytically predicted exponential growth.
infographic.watch_item: Growth requires a stress gradient and shear above a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities; applicability outside these conditions remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence

title: Fourier-Feature-Embedded Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Convolutional Residual Networks for Sparse and Gappy Noisy Flow-Field Reconstruction
authors: Biswanath Barman, Rajendra K. Ray
abstract: Reconstructing flow fields from sparse and noisy measurements becomes particularly challenging when data are completely absent from dynamically critical regions, such as the vortex-formation region of a wake. Conventional interpolation and numerical reconstruction methods generally require sufficient spatial or boundary information, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can also face difficulties when sparse and noisy observations provide little or no supervision in the region of interest. To address this gap, we propose a Fourier-feature-embedded complex-valued physics-informed convolutional residual network (FCV-PICRN) for sparse, gappy, and noisy flow-field reconstruction. The framework integrates Fourier features for oscillatory and multiscale structures, complex-valued representations for coupled amplitude--phase learning, and convolutional residual blocks constrained by the Navier--Stokes equations. The method is first verified using the Taylor--Green vortex at $Re=100$ and then evaluated for the cylinder wake at $Re=100$. Three severe missing-data configurations are imposed in the dynamically sensitive wake: a large hole, a large truncation, and a plus-shaped gap extending in both streamwise and transverse directions. These gaps are further combined with additive Gaussian and multiplicative speckle noise. Despite having no supervised velocity data inside the excluded regions, FCV-PICRN reconstructs velocity, pressure, and vorticity with high structural similarity index (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and remains robust under Gaussian noise up to $20\%$. Finally, for forced two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence with $5\%$ Gaussian noise, FCV-PICRN yields lower reconstruction errors than a conventional PINN. These results demonstrate robust physics-informed reconstruction of severely incomplete and noisy flows across laminar and turbulent regimes.

infographic.key_insight: FCV-PICRN reconstructs flow structures across large unsupervised gaps by combining Fourier features, complex-valued learning, and Navier–Stokes constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could improve flow-field estimation when measurements are sparse, noisy, or unavailable in critical wake regions.
method: Fourier features represent oscillatory and multiscale flow structures.
Complex-valued convolutional residual blocks learn coupled amplitude–phase representations.
Navier–Stokes constraints guide reconstruction where supervised velocity data are absent.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests covered Taylor–Green and cylinder-wake flows at Re=100, three severe gap geometries, robustness under up to 20% Gaussian noise, and lower errors than a conventional PINN for 2D Kolmogorov turbulence with 5% Gaussian noise.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to three-dimensional, higher-Reynolds-number flows and computational cost are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Fourier-Feature-Embedded Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Convolutional Residual Networks for Sparse and Gappy Noisy Flow-Field Reconstruction

title: Reduced graph-based representations of detonation-containing flows
authors: Sinaendhran Pujali Elilarasan, Michael Ullman, Shivam Barwey
abstract: A graph neural network (GNN)-based autoencoder is leveraged to produce reduced latent graph representations of detonation-containing flows. In a two-dimensional hydrogen-air channel configuration with a uniform fuel-air mixture, it was found that latent graphs with effective resolutions of twice the induction length are capable of reconstructing both the wavefront and the post-shock region of the cellular detonation wave structure. Extrapolation studies using stratified and three-dimensional detonation configurations revealed an intrinsic property of GNN-based reconstruction from reduced latent graphs -- a representational hierarchy, rooted in the local nature of message passing, that tends to prioritize features at the detonation front (i.e., the wavefront profile and triple points) over the downstream deflagrative regions. In particular, it was found that at a fixed ambient condition, the information contained in uniform two-dimensional detonations was sufficient to reconstruct the wavefront structure of both stratified and three-dimensional detonations. Overall, this work demonstrates the utility of GNNs for both reduction and information overlap extraction in detonation-containing flows, opening promising pathways for accelerated simulations of these flows.

infographic.key_insight: A GNN autoencoder compresses detonation flows into latent graphs while preferentially preserving wavefront profiles and triple points over downstream deflagrative structures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact graph representations could support accelerated detonation simulations by retaining key wavefront features across different flow configurations.
method: Encode detonation flow fields into reduced latent graphs using a GNN autoencoder.
Reconstruct cellular detonation structures through local message passing.
Evaluate extrapolation from uniform 2D hydrogen–air detonations to stratified and 3D configurations.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the uniform 2D case, latent graphs with effective resolution twice the induction length reconstructed the wavefront and post-shock region; extrapolation at fixed ambient conditions retained wavefront structure in stratified and 3D detonations.
infographic.watch_item: Reconstruction favors wavefront features over downstream deflagrative regions, so fidelity across the full flow field should be checked before simulation use.
infographic.paper_title: Reduced graph-based representations of detonation-containing flows

title: Fully resolved particle dynamics over long time scales in acoustofluidic flows: Theory and numerical simulations
authors: Khemraj Gautam Kshetri, Amneet Pal Singh Bhalla, Nitesh Nama
abstract: We present a perturbation-based theoretical framework, together with its immersed boundary/volume penalization implementation, for long-time simulations of fully resolved rigid-particle dynamics in acoustically actuated flows. A perturbation formulation separates the fast acoustic time scale from the slow mean dynamics, avoiding long-time direct integration of the fully compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The immersed rigid body is represented through a Brinkman penalization term in equations posed over a unified fluid-solid domain. The coupled fluid-particle system is decomposed into a time-harmonic first-order problem governing the acoustic response and a time-averaged second-order problem. A central challenge in this decomposition is the treatment of the moving fluid-solid interface. We derive order-consistent expressions for the structural velocities, comprising rigid-body and Stokes-drift contributions, and formulate the corresponding first- and second-order rigid-body equations of motion. For a circular particle in two dimensions, the simulations reveal substantial differences in the magnitude and structure of acoustic streaming around fixed and freely moving particles, highlighting the importance of two-way fluid-structure coupling. The results also show that particle-density effects are more complex than suggested by simplified descriptions based solely on the acoustic contrast factor. The framework captures the mean particle dynamics using time steps associated with the slow particle-motion scale rather than the much smaller acoustic time scale. Finally, simulations of an elliptical particle demonstrate the ability of the method to capture coupled translational and rotational motion. The proposed approach therefore provides an efficient route to fully resolved, long-time simulations of acoustically driven rigid-particle motion while retaining two-way fluid-structure coupling.

infographic.key_insight: Separating fast acoustics from slow mean motion enables long-time, fully resolved particle simulations while retaining two-way fluid–structure coupling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could improve acoustofluidic particle-manipulation predictions by resolving density-dependent motion, streaming, and particle rotation.
method: Split dynamics into time-harmonic first-order acoustics and time-averaged second-order flow.
Represent rigid particles using immersed-boundary/Brinkman volume penalization.
Derive order-consistent particle velocities and equations of motion, including Stokes drift.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two-dimensional circular-particle simulations show substantial streaming differences between fixed and freely moving particles, while elliptical-particle simulations demonstrate coupled translation and rotation.
infographic.watch_item: Moving-interface consistency is a key implementation concern; the abstract reports no quantitative error or speedup benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: Fully resolved particle dynamics over long time scales in acoustofluidic flows: Theory and numerical simulations

title: Load-Balanced Neural-Network-Aided Adaptive Tabulation of Phase Equilibria for Transcritical Multiphase Flows
authors: Navneeth Srinivasan, Po-Yu Lai, Suo Yang
abstract: Simulating high-pressure transcritical flows with phase change is critical for advanced propulsion, yet traditional first-principles approaches, vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) calculations, consume most of the runtime and frequently fail to converge. Standalone machine learning models introduce heavy evaluation overhead across large grids, while dynamic tabulation still relies on fragile iterative solvers. To resolve these limitations, this study introduces a hybrid In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation and Artificial Neural Network (ISAT-ANN) framework. A pre-trained ANN replaces the iterative solver during table expansion to guarantee crash-free operation, while ISAT enables rapid data retrieval via local linear interpolation. To eliminate parallel load imbalances, an O(N) greedy load-balancing algorithm redistributes computational tasks across cores. Coupled with Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), the framework was validated on a Mach 5 shock-droplet interaction benchmark. It accurately captured shock-interface dynamics without instability, achieving a 2.30 times speedup in thermodynamic calculations on a single core and 2.62 times in parallel over standalone ANNs, with AMR providing an additional 2.92 times overall efficiency boost. This plug-and-play framework offers a stable, scalable path for high-fidelity multiphase flow simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Combining neural-network phase-equilibrium predictions with adaptive tabulation accelerates thermodynamic calculations while avoiding fragile iterative VLE solves.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports stable, scalable simulations of high-pressure transcritical multiphase flows relevant to advanced propulsion.
method: Use a pretrained ANN for phase-equilibrium evaluations during ISAT table expansion.
Retrieve tabulated states rapidly through local linear interpolation.
Redistribute tasks with an O(N) greedy load balancer and integrate adaptive mesh refinement.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a Mach 5 shock–droplet benchmark, the abstract reports accurate shock–interface dynamics without instability, thermodynamic speedups of 2.30× on one core and 2.62× in parallel versus standalone ANNs, plus a separate 2.92× overall efficiency boost from AMR.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is reported for one benchmark; accuracy and stability beyond the ANN training domain require further assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Load-Balanced Neural-Network-Aided Adaptive Tabulation of Phase Equilibria for Transcritical Multiphase Flows

title: A Neural Implicit Flow Super-Resolution Approach for Reacting Flows
authors: Dakshaka Vishwajith Amarathunga, Lanre M. Oshinowo, Ji-Woong Park, Tarek Echekki
abstract: We present a novel framework for reconstructing fine-resolution scalar fields from coarse-resolution data in 2D unsteady flames using an extension of neural implicit flow (NIF). The framework leverages the novel architecture of NIF to develop an efficient representation of scalar fields in spatio-temporal reacting flows. Different strategies are adopted within the proposed framework to establish super-resolution for multiscalar fields in combustion. They include 1) a reconfiguration of the input and output fields, 2) the use of a latent composition space based on nonlinear principal component analysis (NLPCA) to reconstruct the fine-resolution fields, and the conversion from nonlinear principal components (NLPCs) to species and temperature contours, and 3) the adoption of multiple ParameterNets in the NIF architecture, each accommodating one of the NLPCs. The framework was validated on a 2D unsteady Bunsen-stabilized lean premixed methane-air flame with forcing at the inlet. The results, using a coarsening ratio of 8 in a given direction, show that the adoption of multiple ParameterNets yields more accurate super-resolution than a single ParameterNet without any additional cost in the hyperparameters.

infographic.key_insight: Using multiple ParameterNets in neural implicit flow improves reacting-flow super-resolution accuracy over a single ParameterNet without increasing the reported hyperparameter cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports reconstruction of fine-resolution species and temperature fields from coarse combustion data.
method: Reconfigure neural implicit flow inputs and outputs for multiscalar super-resolution.
Use nonlinear principal component analysis to represent composition in a latent space and reconstruct species and temperature fields.
Assign a separate ParameterNet to each nonlinear principal component.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation on a 2D unsteady, inlet-forced, lean premixed methane–air Bunsen flame used a coarsening ratio of 8 in a given direction and favored multiple ParameterNets.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to 3D flames, other fuels, and different combustion regimes is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A Neural Implicit Flow Super-Resolution Approach for Reacting Flows

title: Dramatic pressure-induced slowdown and the soft glassy rheology of water at 2D material interface
authors: Guilhem Mariette, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Jean Comtet
abstract: The flow of molecularly confined water has attracted considerable interest in recent years. Yet despite their exquisite character, current nanofluidic devices cannot probe molecular water flow beyond the linear-response regime, while nanomechanical force- based approaches have produced markedly inconsistent results. Here, using tuning- fork-based atomic force microscopy, we tackle these limitations by measuring the full linear-to-nonlinear, shear-dependent viscoelastic rheology of molecularly confined water at various two-dimensional material interfaces -- demonstrating pronounced rate effects in water flow response. The observed rheological behaviors are remarkably analogous to that of macroscopic soft glassy yielding materials and fully captured by a non-linear model accounting for the shear-induced acceleration of the dynamics -- a hallmark of disordered supercooled and metastable systems. We further unveil a pronounced pressure-induced slowdown in nanoconfined water dynamics, with relaxation times extending into the microsecond range and marked material dependence. These results reveal non-linear, glassy rheology as a general feature of interfacial water and offer a route to tunable, non-linear nanofluidic elements.

infographic.key_insight: Molecularly confined water at 2D material interfaces exhibits nonlinear, soft-glassy rheology and a pressure-induced slowdown with relaxation times reaching microseconds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Pressure- and material-dependent water dynamics could enable tunable nonlinear nanofluidic elements.
method: Use tuning-fork-based atomic force microscopy to probe confined water.
Measure shear-dependent viscoelasticity from linear to nonlinear response across different 2D interfaces.
Model the response using shear-induced acceleration of relaxation dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Measurements reveal pronounced rate effects, microsecond relaxation times, and material-dependent dynamics, with the observed rheology captured by a nonlinear model.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative pressure ranges or device-scale validation, limiting assessment of practical operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Dramatic pressure-induced slowdown and the soft glassy rheology of water at 2D material interface

title: How stagnation lines move, persist and break up in fluid flows
authors: Prabakaran Rajamanickam
abstract: Stagnation curves of arbitrary shape (zeros of $\mathbf v(\mathbf x,t)$) are non-generic yet common; we derive their motion. Differentiating $\mathbf v=\mathbf0$ gives $\mathbf L\mathbf U=-\mathbf a$ ($\mathbf U$ curve velocity, $\mathbf a=\mathbf v_t$, $\mathbf L=\nabla\mathbf v$ kills tangent, acts on normal plane via $2\times2$ block $\mathbf K$); dynamics enters only via $\mathbf a$. Normal velocity: $-\mathbf K^{-1}$ times normal $\mathbf a$; tangential solvability: scalar condition $Σ=0$ per point ($Σ$: part of $\mathbf a$ outside range $\mathbf L$). Potential flow: $\mathbf K$ is strain rate, normal velocity pressure gradient over principal strain rate $ε$, persistence needs uniform pressure on it. Stokes flow: tangential vorticity enters $\mathbf K$ (centre lines), $Σ$ involves normal vorticity. Navier-Stokes: $Σ$ set by instantaneous flow via nonlocal pressure, viscosity. If $Σ\ne0$, line becomes, to first order in $t$, isolated points at zeros of $Σ$ (critical points of $\varphi_t$ if potential; maybe none in Stokes flow: loops vanish). Symmetry (line an orbit of rigid-motion group, no velocity along it) suffices for persistence, not necessary: flows steady in rigidly moving frame have $Σ\equiv0$. Incompressibility enters via $\mathrm{tr}\mathbf K=0$; for inviscid irrotational homentropic compressible flow, line dilatation is $\varphi_{tt}/c^2$, so lines can be nodes, persistence needs uniform enthalpy, singular $\mathbf K$ arises at ordinary points, acoustic standing waves give exact examples (node line breaking into alternating sinks, saddles); also degenerate $\mathbf K$ (pairs born at distance $O(\sqrt t)$), curvature, torsion evolution, closure for moving-singularity-driven flows, helical and elliptically conical stagnation-point flow, exact Navier-Stokes example: saddle, centre lines split into four points per period.

infographic.key_insight: Stagnation lines persist only when local flow acceleration satisfies a scalar compatibility condition; otherwise, they generally break into isolated stagnation points.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can help diagnose the motion and breakup of zero-velocity structures in simulated flows without assuming that stagnation lines persist.
method: Differentiate the zero-velocity condition to relate line motion to local acceleration and the velocity gradient.
Invert the normal-plane velocity-gradient block to obtain normal motion and test a scalar persistence condition.
Apply the framework to potential, Stokes, Navier–Stokes and compressible flows, including degenerate cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical derivations and exact examples, including acoustic standing waves and Navier–Stokes stagnation lines splitting into four points per period, rather than experimental or numerical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The normal-velocity formula requires an invertible normal-plane gradient block; singular cases need separate analysis and can produce square-root-in-time point separation.
infographic.paper_title: How stagnation lines move, persist and break up in fluid flows

title: Influence of Droplet Morphology on Fluid Dynamics and Impact Erosion of Wind Turbine Blades
authors: Hao Hao, Antonis Sergis, Maria N. Charalambides, Alex M. K. P. Taylor, Yannis Hardalupas
abstract: The impact of droplets, such as rain and sea sprays, on wind turbine blade surfaces can cause severe damage through leading-edge erosion (LEE). Current industrial practice has largely relied on empirical fatigue models to predict damage progression and guide maintenance. However, an important limitation of existing models is the assumption on ideal impact conditions, including perfectly spherical droplet and normal incidence, which rarely occur in reality. This study develops a fluid-structure interaction (FSI) model that couples incompressible multiphase flow simulations with finite element (FE) analysis of blade materials. Using this framework, we investigate the impact dynamics of droplets with arbitrary shapes and orientations. The results reveal a positive correlation between the peak impact pressure, the influential area at the pressure peak, and the peak impact force. In contrast, the time of peak force scales inversely due to momentum conservation. From these findings, we propose a $\textit{universal scaling law}$ that relates all key impact loadings to the simple parameter of the droplet $\textit{projection area}$, which can be determined solely from the initial droplet geometry and orientation. This law provides a predictive framework for impact loading dynamics of non-ideal shapes, offering new insights into the mechanisms of LEE and improving the accuracy of erosion predictions for wind turbine blades.

infographic.key_insight: A proposed universal scaling law links droplet projection area to key impact loads, capturing the effects of initial droplet shape and orientation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could improve wind turbine leading-edge erosion predictions beyond idealized spherical-droplet, normal-incidence assumptions.
method: Couple incompressible multiphase flow simulations with finite element analysis through fluid–structure interaction.
Investigate impact dynamics for droplets with arbitrary shapes and orientations.
Relate impact-loading metrics to projection area determined from initial droplet geometry.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show positively correlated peak pressure, affected area at peak pressure, and peak force, with peak-force timing scaling inversely; the abstract provides no quantitative accuracy metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish experimental validation or the scaling law’s applicability across real blade materials and operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Influence of Droplet Morphology on Fluid Dynamics and Impact Erosion of Wind Turbine Blades

title: Wavepackets in subsonic elliptical jets: coherent-structure eduction and linear modelling
authors: Filipe Ramos do Amaral, Mateus Peixoto Avanci, Jean-Christophe Robinet, Peter Jordan, Jérôme Huber, Grégoire Pont
abstract: We study coherent structures extracted from time-resolved particle image velocimetry (TR-PIV) measurements of isothermal elliptical jets with aspect ratio of 1:2, at Mach numbers 0.4 and 0.7. The velocity snapshots are decomposed according to the D$_2$ symmetry. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) is then used to identify coherent structures. Modelling is performed using three-dimensional parabolised stability equations (3D-PSE) based on linearisation about the time-averaged mean flows. A comparison between SPOD and 3D-PSE results shows alignment of SPOD and single-mode PSE structures of up to 70\%. A linear combination of PSE solutions, obtained from the family of initially unstable local modes, leads to SPOD-PSE alignment of up to 90\%. Limitations are observed at low frequencies and near the nozzle and are attributed to the existence of non-modal amplification mechanisms. The study shows that coherent structures in turbulent elliptical jets can be educed using the D$_2$-SPOD approach, and modelled using 3D PSE.

infographic.key_insight: Symmetry-aware SPOD reveals coherent wavepackets in elliptical jets, with combinations of linear 3D-PSE modes achieving up to 90% alignment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Linear 3D-PSE modelling offers a physics-based route to representing coherent structures in turbulent, non-axisymmetric jets.
method: Decompose time-resolved PIV velocity snapshots using D₂ symmetry.
Extract coherent structures with spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD).
Compare SPOD structures with single and combined 3D-PSE modes linearised about measured mean flows.
infographic.evidence_signal: For isothermal jets with 1:2 aspect ratio at Mach 0.4 and 0.7, SPOD–PSE alignment reached up to 70% for single modes and 90% for mode combinations.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement is limited at low frequencies and near the nozzle, where non-modal amplification may matter.
infographic.paper_title: Wavepackets in subsonic elliptical jets: coherent-structure eduction and linear modelling

title: Second-order difference-frequency effects on floating wind turbine responses: full-QTF modelling and experimental comparison
authors: Yi Zhang, Tom Tosdevin, Tianning Tang, Peter Stansby
abstract: Accurate prediction of low-frequency responses is important for the dynamic assessment of floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs), as second-order difference-frequency wave loads can contribute substantially to platform motions and mooring loads. Their relative importance, however, remains less well established when aerodynamic and hydrodynamic low-frequency excitations coexist under operating conditions. This study develops an efficient time-domain formulation for full difference-frequency quadratic transfer function (QTF) loading using bandwidth truncation and integrates it into a fully coupled model of the IEA 15 MW turbine on the VolturnUS-S semi-submersible platform. Numerical predictions are compared with 1:70-scale real-time hybrid wave-basin experiments covering both irregular wave-only and combined turbulent wind-wave conditions. Three hydrodynamic formulations are compared: linear wave excitation, Newman's approximation, and the full-QTF model. Under wave-only conditions, second-order difference-frequency loading substantially improves the prediction of surge and the associated mooring response, particularly in energetic sea states, with the full-QTF model generally providing the closest agreement with measured low-frequency spectra and peak-amplitude distributions. Under combined wind-wave conditions, low-frequency thrust fluctuations dominate near rated wind speed, reducing the relative importance of difference-frequency wave excitation, whereas its contribution becomes more apparent at higher wind speeds as thrust fluctuations diminish. Overall, the full-QTF model provides the most consistent improvement over the linear and Newman models, with maximum surge standard deviation discrepancy from measurement under the most energetic wave conditions less than 18%, with smaller discrepancies for heave, pitch, and mooring tensions.

infographic.key_insight: Full difference-frequency QTF loading improves floating wind turbine response predictions most consistently, especially for wave-driven low-frequency surge and mooring loads.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Including second-order wave loads can improve platform-motion and mooring-load assessments, although their relative importance depends on operating wind conditions.
method: Develop an efficient time-domain full-QTF formulation using bandwidth truncation.
Integrate it into a fully coupled IEA 15 MW turbine–VolturnUS-S platform model.
Compare linear excitation, Newman's approximation, and full-QTF predictions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Comparisons with 1:70-scale hybrid wave-basin experiments under wave-only and turbulent wind–wave conditions showed full-QTF surge standard deviation discrepancies below 18% in the most energetic wave conditions, with smaller discrepancies for heave, pitch, and mooring tensions.
infographic.watch_item: The reported validation covers one turbine–platform configuration at model scale, so generalization to other systems and full-scale conditions requires further evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Second-order difference-frequency effects on floating wind turbine responses: full-QTF modelling and experimental comparison

title: NeRF-Inspired Neural Fields for 3D Super-resolution of Reacting-Flows
authors: Dakshaka Vishwajith Amarathunga, Shang-Ru Li, Tarek Echekki
abstract: The multiscale nature of turbulent reacting flows and the importance of fine-scale structures pose challenges for super-resolution. We investigate a 3D super-resolution framework inspired by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), called Neural Field Super-Resolution (NFSR), to reconstruct fine-resolution fields from coarsened reacting-flow fields. The proposed formulation adapts the continuous coordinate-conditioned representation of NeRF to physical flow-field reconstruction by conditioning spatial coordinates with local coarse-grid thermochemical information, while eliminating radiance prediction and volume rendering. Principal component analysis is used to provide a compact and low-dimensional representation of the thermochemical state, and a hierarchical extension, H-NFSR, progressively reconstructs the solution through intermediate resolution levels. The framework is evaluated using three-dimensional direct numerical simulation data for a turbulent premixed hydrogen-air flame, with an overall spatial coarsening factor of eight in each coordinate direction. The results demonstrate consistently better prediction measures and a higher ability to reconstruct fine-scale information than tricubic interpolation on the unseen test realization. The hierarchical formulation reduces visible coarse-cell imprinting. In contrast, biased sampling mainly benefits the most localized structures. Three-dimensional isosurface comparisons further show that H-NFSR recovers much of the small and intermediate features of the flow, including surface wrinkling and local flame curvature effects. These results highlight the potential of coordinate-conditioned neural fields as a flexible framework for three-dimensional coarse-to-fine reconstruction of reacting-flow simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Coordinate-conditioned neural fields reconstruct fine-scale 3D reacting-flow structures better than tricubic interpolation, while hierarchical reconstruction reduces coarse-cell imprinting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help recover flame wrinkling and local curvature from coarse reacting-flow fields for more detailed engineering analysis.
method: Condition spatial coordinates on local coarse-grid thermochemical information, without radiance prediction or volume rendering.
Compress the thermochemical state using principal component analysis.
Progressively reconstruct intermediate resolution levels with hierarchical NFSR.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 3D DNS data for a turbulent premixed hydrogen–air flame coarsened eightfold per coordinate direction, NFSR outperformed tricubic interpolation on an unseen test realization.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the evaluated flame configuration remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: NeRF-Inspired Neural Fields for 3D Super-resolution of Reacting-Flows
